sentences.text: This dinosaur reached a length of about 11 meters, which is shorter than many other sauropods.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul calculated its mass at 3.5 tonnes.
Its sturdy, pillar-like forelimbs were 76% the length of its hind legs.
The animal had a sacrum formed by four fused vertebrae, unlike prosauropods which had only three.
As a quadrupedal herbivore, it followed the standard sauropod design with long necks and tails.
At roughly 11 meters long, this creature was notably smaller than most of its sauropod relatives.
Gregory S. Paul estimated its weight to be 3.5 tonnes in 2010.
Michael Raath named the genus in 1972 after finding the first bone in July 1969 in Zimbabwe.
The fossils come from a single site on an island within Lake Kariba, the largest man-made lake.
Raath originally classified it as a specialized prosauropod rather than a sauropod.
Early researchers believed the animal was omnivorous because of knife-shaped teeth found near the fossils.
Later studies revealed those sharp teeth belonged to a scavenging theropod, not the sauropod itself.
Raath suggested in 1972 that the carcass lay in a death pose with the neck bent backward over the pelvis.
Cooper noted in 1984 that the desert-like environment proved the animal was terrestrial, not aquatic.
Arthur Cruickshank proved in 1975 that it was a true sauropod, and it is now seen as a basal member of the group.
Michael Cooper created the family Vulcanodontidae in 1984, but Paul Upchurch showed in 1995 that this grouping was invalid.
Some analyses link it with Tazoudasaurus, though this relationship remains debated among scientists.
The species lived during the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages, spanning from 199.5 to 184.2 million years ago.
Adam Yates confirmed in 2004 that the fossils date to the Toarcian stage, between 175 and 183 million years ago.
The remains were found in the Vulcanodon beds, a sediment unit inside the Batoka Formation made mostly of flood basalts.
